vignette:
He is 53 now, a city bus driver who has spent most of his adult life moving other people safely from one stop to the next. He is married, the kind of man who used to measure his worth by being dependable: up before dawn, coffee poured into a travel mug, route memorized, bills paid on time, snow shoveled before his wife wakes. When he talks about who he was before, he does it indirectly, through routines. He says he “used to not think twice” about working late, about taking an extra shift, about walking through a dark depot parking lot without checking over his shoulder.

The assault happens three years ago after an evening shift. He has parked his bus and is finishing the end-of-day paperwork in a mostly empty terminal. A man he vaguely recognizes from the station hangs back and asks him a question, then follows him toward the employee washroom corridor. The patient remembers the fluorescent lights, one of them flickering, and the sharp chemical smell of disinfectant. He remembers confusion first—thinking this is some kind of robbery, that he can hand over his wallet and go home. What happens instead feels impossible even now when he tells it. He is overpowered, trapped, and raped. He says the worst part is not only the pain and fear but the instant collapse of his own assumptions about himself. He had always believed that if danger came, he would fight harder, yell louder, do something decisive. Instead he freezes, then obeys, his mind narrowing to fragments: the floor, the sound of a door, his own breathing turning strange and far away.

Afterward he drives home in a state he describes as “not really in the truck.” He does not tell his wife that night. He showers for a long time, scrubbing until his skin burns, then lies awake staring at the ceiling. In the morning he goes to work. He tells himself that if he keeps his route, keeps his hands on the wheel, maybe the event will flatten into something unreal. Instead the world changes shape. Every man who boards the bus alone late at night gets scanned as a possible threat. He watches hands, posture, exits. At red lights he checks the side mirrors not just for traffic but for people approaching too fast.

He avoids the terminal corridor where it happened, then starts avoiding the entire end of the depot. He trades shifts to stay on daylight routes. When dispatch changes his schedule unexpectedly, he feels a surge of panic so strong he has to grip the steering wheel until his fingers cramp. Once, a passenger stands too close behind him while asking about a transfer and he jerks so violently that the man steps back, offended. He apologizes, but for the rest of the route his shirt is damp with sweat and he can feel his heart pounding in his throat.

At home, his wife knows something is wrong long before he tells her. He becomes irritable in ways that confuse them both. Small noises make him snap. He starts checking the locks two and three times before bed. He cannot tolerate being touched unexpectedly, even by her, and then hates himself for flinching. Their marriage narrows around what he cannot explain. He sleeps in short stretches and wakes from nightmares with the feeling of someone pinning him down. Sometimes he comes fully awake swinging his arms, then sits on the edge of the bed shaking, unable to separate the dream from the room around him.

Telling his wife is one of the hardest things he has done. He expects disbelief, or worse, pity. He circles around it for weeks, speaking first about “something bad” at work, then finally forcing the words out in a flat, mechanical voice. He cannot look at her while he says it. What stays with him afterward is not anything she says wrong, because she does not say anything wrong, but the look of grief on her face. He feels exposed, ashamed, and furious that the assault has entered the house and sits between them.

He tries to carry on, but his life becomes organized around avoidance and vigilance. He turns down social invitations. He no longer stops for coffee with the other drivers before a shift because locker-room joking and casual physical closeness feel intolerable. He feels cut off from other men in particular, as if he has been moved outside some category he once belonged to. He thinks often, in unwanted flashes, of the assault: while cleaning the bus, while hearing footsteps behind him, while smelling industrial cleanser in a public restroom. The memories do not arrive like ordinary remembering. They hit with full force, and for a few seconds he is back there, body rigid, breath shallow, the present gone.

He speaks about himself now with a harshness that is striking. He calls himself weak, damaged, not the husband he was. Yet beneath that is a man still trying to function, still driving his route, still nodding to regular passengers, still making it home each night. He sits in the office describing how exhausting it is to live as if danger is always one step behind him. What troubles him most is that the assault did not stay in the past. It keeps happening in his body, in his marriage, in the split second before someone comes too close, and in every ordinary moment that no longer feels ordinary at all.
